Now I am needing to see the correleation between all features that I scrapped and added to see if there are some features that I can drop¶

In [336]:
sns.set(rc={'figure.figsize':(20,15)})
sns.heatmap(df.corr(numeric_only=True), annot=True)
Out[336]:
<Axes: >

Heatmap Analysis¶

The heatmap shows a very strong correlation between the first three features and the team's final league position. These features appear to represent closely related and relatively direct aspects of team performance, which could make their relationship with league position somewhat obvious.

Since the main objective of this project is to investigate which factors are associated with a team's league position and, in particular, what characteristics may contribute to becoming champion, I decided to remove the highly correlated feature. Keeping all of these closely related variables could cause the model to rely heavily on these obvious performance indicators, making it more difficult to identify the contribution of other, less obvious features.

Therefore, I will remove this feature to reduce redundancy and encourage the model to consider a broader range of factors when analysing which characteristics are associated with a team's success and final position in the league.

Added Redudancy¶

When I mutiplied and sumed the goals percentage by matches played and I created a new column I added redundancy, it gave me 1 which mean that are the same and affect in a same way the model, that is why I am going to revert it

In [337]:

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=1)

model = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100, random_state=10)

model.fit(X_train, y_train)

predict = model.predict(X_test)

comparasion  = pd.DataFrame({'Actual': y_test, 'Predicted': predict})

print(comparasion)

model_score = model.score(X_test, y_test)

print(f'Model Score: {model_score}')

print(f'Mean Absolute Error: {mean_absolute_error(y_test, predict)}')

Problem Hypothesis¶

The first data frame is unbalaced and can be cause that the score is a little bit misleading.

Solution¶

I am going validate them using cross-validation to see how are the results in general

In [351]:
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

score_model = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5)

score_model_120 = cross_val_score(model_120, X_120, y_120, cv=5)

print(f"Cross-validation scores for the original dataset: {score_model}")

print(f"Cross-validation scores for the 120 dataset: {score_model_120}")

Results Analysis¶

The model trained with 120 samples is way better to understand general data and it is more balaced at the time to predict positions
